title: Mechanics of Options Markets: Payoffs, Moneyness, and Contract Adjustments
prerequisites: Basic equity market mechanics and share pricing (S)
Fundamental concept of financial derivatives and forward contracts
Elementary algebra and piecewise maximum functions max(a, b)
learningOutcomes: Distinguish between call and put options, European and American exercise styles, and the asymmetric rights versus obligations of buyers and sellers ([fact-01]).
Calculate and graph gross payoffs and net profits at expiration for all four foundational option positions: long call, short call, long put, and short put ([fact-02], [fact-03], [fact-04]).
Evaluate real-world 100-share option contracts using Google case studies and classify options into ITM, ATM, and OTM moneyness states ([fact-05], [fact-06], [fact-07]).
Identify North American exchange-traded contract specifications, including expiration cycles, strike intervals, position limits, and 5-day exercise limits ([fact-08], [fact-09]).
Compute exact strike price and contract deliverable adjustments for N-for-M stock splits, stock dividends, and extraordinary special cash dividends such as the Gucci takeover ([fact-10], [fact-11]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Exercising an ITM call generates a positive gross payoff max(S_T - K, 0), but net profit requires subtracting the upfront premium c ([fact-02], [fact-05]). In the Google long call example (K = $550, c = $29.00), if S_T is between $550.01 and $578.99, the gross payoff is positive, yet it is less than the $2,900 upfront outlay, resulting in a net loss ([fact-05]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Exchange-traded options are never adjusted for ordinary cash dividends ([fact-10]). Adjustments occur only for stock splits, stock dividends ([fact-10]), or extraordinarily large special cash dividends—such as Gucci Group NV's $13.50 per share special dividend during the 2000-2001 LVMH/PPR takeover battle ([fact-11]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Position limits aggregate contracts on the same directional side of the market, not long versus short contracts ([fact-09]). The bullish side sums Long Calls + Short Puts, while the bearish side sums Short Calls + Long Puts ([fact-09]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A trader holds 1 standard contract (100 shares) of a call option with strike price K = $60. The company executes a 3-for-2 non-round-lot stock split, and also pays an ordinary quarterly cash dividend of $0.50 per share. Meanwhile, another trader sells 1 September put contract on Google (100 shares) at strike K = $525 for a bid premium of p = $22.40 per share, and Google closes at S_T = $480 at expiration.
activeRecallQuiz.question: What are the adjusted contract terms for the $60 call option after the 3-for-2 split and ordinary dividend, and what are the exact gross loss and net loss for the Google short put writer at S_T = $480?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Options grant holders the right without obligation to buy (call) or sell (put) at strike K in exchange for premium c or p, creating capped downside for buyers and asymmetric obligations for writers ([fact-01], [fact-02], [fact-03], [fact-04]).

Gross payoff at expiration measures only intrinsic exercise value max(S_T - K, 0) or max(K - S_T, 0), whereas net profit deducts or adds the initial 100-share contract premium outlay or inflow ([fact-02], [fact-05], [fact-06], [fact-07]).

North American exchange-traded options follow standardized 100-share lots, expiration cycles, and same-side position/exercise limits ([fact-08], [fact-09]), adjusting strike and share terms for N-for-M splits, stock dividends, and extraordinary special dividends like Gucci's $13.50 payout, but never for ordinary cash dividends ([fact-10], [fact-11]).
